title: Testing and code quality
blurb: Unit vs integration, test doubles, what makes a test brittle, and how to answer 'what's your testing strategy' without bluffing.

questions.q: What makes a function easy to test?
choices: It is short, ideally under ten lines, so one test covers the whole body
It is pure: the same input gives the same output, with no side effects
It lives in its own file, so the test can import it and nothing else
It takes no parameters, so there are no input combinations left to test
questions.why: No setup, no mocks, no cleanup: call it and assert. That is why 'separate deciding from doing' is a testability strategy, not just style. A short function that reads the clock or the database still needs all of that setup.
questions.asked: An opener that leads into how you structure code so the logic can be tested without infrastructure.

questions.q: What is the difference between a unit test and an integration test?
choices: A unit test is written by developers; an integration test is written by the QA team
A unit test checks one piece alone; an integration test checks pieces working together
A unit test runs in CI on every push; an integration test runs on a developer's machine
A unit test calls a function directly; an integration test always drives the UI
questions.why: The boundary is a judgement call; a test hitting a real database is integration by most definitions. What matters is what each catches: unit tests catch logic errors, integration tests catch wiring errors. Driving the UI is an end-to-end test.
questions.asked: A definition every interviewer checks before asking about your own testing strategy.

questions.q: What is the usual criticism of the testing pyramid (many unit, fewer integration, few end-to-end tests)?
choices: It puts end-to-end tests at the base, which makes the whole suite slow, flaky and costly to run
It only applies to backend services, so frontends get no guidance from it
Mocked unit tests can all pass while the wiring between units, where bugs ship, is broken
It forbids integration tests, so database bugs are only found in production
questions.why: The 'testing trophy' argument: most real defects live in the wiring between units, so a suite of heavily mocked unit tests can be green while the app is broken. Either shape is defensible if you can explain what it buys.
questions.asked: 'What's your testing strategy?': this is where a considered opinion beats a diagram.

questions.q: What is the difference between a stub and a mock?
choices: A stub is generated by a library, while a mock is always written by hand for the test
A mock replaces a whole database, while a stub replaces only a single function
A stub is used only in unit tests, while a mock is used only in integration tests
A stub returns canned values; a mock also verifies it was called in an expected way
questions.why: Mocks couple the test to how the code works. Asserting 'saveUser was called once with X' breaks on a legitimate refactor; asserting on the resulting state does not. Both can be hand-written or generated, at any test level.
questions.asked: The follow-up is when you would prefer asserting state over verifying calls.

questions.q: What makes a test brittle?
choices: It asserts on implementation details rather than on observable behaviour
It reads real data from a fixture file instead of values built inside the test
It runs for several seconds, so developers skip it when testing locally
It has more than one assertion, so one small change fails several checks
questions.why: Whole-DOM snapshots, mocks asserting internal call order, tests reaching into private state: they fail on every refactor and stop being trusted. A slow test is a cost, not brittleness, and several assertions about one behaviour are fine.
questions.asked: Tests whether you can explain why a suite gets deleted or ignored, which is the real cost of brittleness.

questions.q: A test passes locally and fails in CI intermittently. What is it most likely to be?
choices: A CI configuration error, since a real bug would fail on every single run
Shared state, order dependence, timing, or time zone and locale assumptions
The test is too slow and CI kills it, which is reported as an assertion failure
A dependency missing from CI that your machine has installed globally
questions.why: Intermittent failures come from tests that depend on each other, on wall-clock timing, on real network calls or on the machine's locale. A missing dependency would fail every run. A flaky test is worse than none: it teaches people to re-run until green.
questions.asked: A scenario question everyone with real experience has an answer to.

questions.q: What does test coverage actually tell you?
choices: How well the code is tested, since every covered line has been verified correct
Roughly how many bugs remain, because uncovered lines are where defects hide
Which lines ran during the tests, not whether the assertions checked anything
Whether every branch is correct, since branch coverage checks each outcome
questions.why: You can reach 100% with tests that assert nothing. Coverage is useful as a floor that points at untested files, and harmful as a target people game. Branch coverage only says both paths ran.
questions.asked: Checks whether you would push back on a coverage target used as a quality metric.

questions.q: What is TDD, in one sentence?
choices: Write the tests after the code, but before the pull request is opened for review
Write a test for every function, including private helpers, before shipping
Design the full test suite up front, then build features until it all passes
Write a failing test, make it pass with the simplest change, then refactor
questions.why: Red, green, refactor, in small steps. The value is design pressure (you must decide the shape of the code before writing it) and proof that each test can fail. Designing the whole suite up front is the opposite of the small-step loop.
questions.asked: A definition check; the follow-up is whether you actually practise it and when you do not.

questions.q: Why write the failing test first, rather than writing the test after the fix?
choices: A test that has never failed has not been shown to detect the bug it targets
It is faster, because the fix is then written with the test already in place
It raises coverage more than writing the same test after the fix would
Most CI systems reject a fix commit that does not first add a failing test
questions.why: Plenty of tests pass because they assert the wrong thing. Watching it go red and then green proves the link between the test and the behaviour. The same test written afterwards gives identical coverage.
questions.asked: Separates people who have seen a test pass for the wrong reason from people who have not.

questions.q: Should a unit test hit the real database?
choices: Yes; every test should use the real database, since mocks can never be trusted
No; no test at any level should touch a database, only mocked repositories
Only in CI, where a real database exists; locally the very same tests should use a mock instead
No, but integration tests should, because in-memory fakes hide real SQL and constraints
questions.why: EF Core's in-memory provider neither enforces constraints nor translates SQL, so tests can pass against behaviour the real database rejects. A real database in a container (Testcontainers) in the pipeline is the modern answer.
questions.asked: Tests whether you know what in-memory fakes silently skip.

questions.q: What should a good test name communicate?
choices: The name of the function under test, so the test file mirrors the source file
The scenario and the expected outcome, so a failure is clear from the name alone
The ticket number, so the requirement behind the test can be looked up later
The author and the date, so questions about the test go to the right person
questions.why: `rejects_transfer_when_balance_is_insufficient` tells you what broke from the CI summary; `test_transfer_2` means opening the file. A function name alone does not say which behaviour failed.
questions.asked: Interviewers read your tests; names are the first thing they see.

questions.q: What is arrange-act-assert?
choices: A naming convention where each test name lists its arrange, act and assert steps
A structure: set up the state, perform one action, then assert on the result
A mocking style in which every dependency is arranged as a mock before acting
An order for CI stages: prepare the environment, deploy, then run smoke tests
questions.why: One action per test. A test that acts three times and asserts after each is really three tests, and its failure message will not tell you which part broke.
questions.asked: A structure check; strong candidates add "one behaviour per test".

questions.q: What is a property-based test?
choices: Checking that an object's properties have the right types after construction
Asserting an invariant that must hold for many generated inputs, not hand-picked ones
Testing configuration properties, such as each environment's settings file
Generating ordinary example-based tests automatically from each function's type signature
questions.why: 'Reversing a list twice gives the original' or 'the parser round-trips everything the serialiser produces'. The library generates and shrinks inputs, so it finds edge cases you would never have written by hand.
questions.asked: A depth signal; mentioning shrinking to a minimal failing case shows real use.

questions.q: How do you test code that depends on the current time?
choices: Run the test at a fixed time of day in CI, so the clock is always predictable
Use a very short timeout so the time barely changes while the test runs
Make the current time an input, via an injected clock or fake timers, fixed in the test
Compare dates with a tolerance of one whole day, so any time of day gives the same test result
questions.why: Treat the ambient clock like any other dependency and control it. An injected clock (.NET 8's `TimeProvider`) and fake timers (`mock.timers` in node:test, `jest.useFakeTimers`) are both implementations of that idea. Scheduling CI at a set hour still breaks on the developer's machine and around daylight saving.
questions.asked: Checks whether you design for testability; tests that fail at midnight are the follow-up.

questions.q: A non-urgent bug is reported in production. Once you understand it, what is the best first step?
choices: Fix it and deploy straight away, then add a test in a follow-up ticket
Add logging around the code and wait for it to happen again to confirm it
Write a failing test that reproduces it, then fix it so the test goes green
Fix it and add a step to the manual QA checklist so each release checks it
questions.why: A regression test is the easiest test to justify: it catches a real bug, because it just did. For an outage the order changes: restore service first by rolling back or mitigating, then write this test as part of the fix.
questions.asked: 'Walk me through how you fix a production bug': the test belongs in the answer, after service is restored if it was an outage.

questions.q: What is the risk of mocking a third-party client heavily?
choices: Mocks run slower than the real client, because every call goes through a proxy
Mocking a library's classes breaches its licence unless you pay for a plan
The mock must be regenerated on every library upgrade, or the build fails to compile at all
Your mock encodes your assumptions, so tests pass even if the real API behaves otherwise
questions.why: The mock agrees with you by construction. Contract tests or a recorded-response fake keep you honest; at minimum, run one integration test against the real service somewhere.
questions.asked: Tests whether you know where mocks stop protecting you.

questions.q: What does code review add that tests do not?
choices: Faster feedback, since a reviewer usually replies before the pipeline has even finished
Judgement on design, naming, missing cases and whether the change should exist
A coverage check, since reviewers confirm each changed line has a test
Formatting consistency, since reviewers catch style that a linter cannot
questions.why: Tests verify the code does what it does. Review asks whether that is the right thing, whether someone will understand it in six months, and whether a case is missing entirely. Style belongs to the formatter.
questions.asked: Checks what you think review is for; nitpicking style is the answer that worries interviewers.

questions.q: What makes a pull request easy to review?
choices: Bundling every related refactor in, so the whole change needs only one review
Splitting it into one PR per file, so each reviewer only reads one file
Keeping tests out of it, so the diff is short and reviewers focus on the code
Small, one concern, a clear what-and-why description, and no unrelated churn
questions.why: Review quality drops sharply with size: a 1,000-line PR gets 'LGTM'. Keep the refactor in a separate commit or PR from the behaviour change so the reviewer can see what actually changed. Splitting by file cuts one concern into pieces nobody can judge alone.
questions.asked: A team-fit question as much as a technical one.

questions.q: When is it reasonable not to write a test?
choices: For a throwaway spike, or trivial code where a test would only restate the implementation
When the deadline is tight, as long as a ticket to add the missing tests goes into the backlog
For UI code, since interface behaviour cannot be tested automatically
When coverage is already above the team's threshold for that module
questions.why: A test asserting that a getter returns its field costs maintenance and catches nothing. Being able to say where tests do not pay is more credible than 'test everything'. UI behaviour is very testable, and 'later' tickets rarely get done.
questions.asked: Tests pragmatism; "never skip tests" and "skip when busy" are both weak answers.

questions.q: What is a smoke test in a deployment pipeline?
choices: The full regression suite, re-run against production after every single deploy
A short load test that checks the new version can handle peak traffic
A security scan of the deployed app for known vulnerable endpoints
A minimal check after deploy that the app is up and its critical path works
questions.why: Hit the health endpoint and one real user journey. It catches the configuration and connectivity failures that no amount of pre-deploy testing can, because they only exist in the target environment.
questions.asked: Connects testing to deployment; the strong answer says what the smoke test would have caught that CI did not.

questions.q: What is the difference between a fake and a spy?
choices: A fake is a working lightweight implementation; a spy records calls for later assertions
A fake throws on every call to prove errors are handled; a spy returns fixed values
A fake is created by a mocking library; a spy is a real object the test cannot change
A fake is used for databases only; a spy is used for HTTP clients and message queues
questions.why: An in-memory repository backed by a Map is a fake: it really stores and returns data. A spy wraps or replaces a function and remembers how it was called. Returning fixed values is a stub.
questions.asked: Vocabulary check before the "when do you use which" discussion.

questions.q: What is the main benefit of a test data builder like `makeUser`?
choices: Tests run faster, because the default object is built once and then cached
Every test gets unique data, so tests can never interfere with each other
Each test states only the fields it cares about, and new fields are added once
Invalid users cannot be created, because it validates against the schema
questions.why: The test for admins says `role: 'admin'` and nothing else, so the reader sees what matters. When the model gains a required field, one builder changes instead of fifty literals. It builds a fresh object on every call and validates nothing.
questions.asked: A signal that you have maintained a large test suite, not just written a few tests.

questions.q: Using boundary value analysis, which ages should the tests for `canVote` include?
choices: 0, 50 and 120, spread evenly across the realistic range of ages
17 and 18, the values on either side of the boundary in the rule
One random age on every run, so the whole range is covered over time
18 and 21, the ages at which voting rules change in most countries
questions.why: Off-by-one bugs live at edges: `>` instead of `>=` passes for 50 and fails only at 18. Testing 17 and 18 pins the exact boundary. Random ages would find it rarely, and not reproducibly.
questions.asked: A classic test-design question; it checks whether you choose inputs deliberately.

questions.q: `getUser` has a bug: for unknown ids it resolves instead of rejecting. What does this node:test test report?
choices: It fails with an assertion error raised by `assert.match`
It passes, because no assertion runs when nothing is thrown
It fails, because the resolved value escapes the try block
It times out, because the catch block is never entered
questions.why: A resolved promise skips the catch, so the test finishes with no assertion and is green. Use `await assert.rejects(getUser(999), /not found/)`, which fails when the promise resolves. Error paths are where tests most often assert nothing.
questions.asked: Tests whether you can spot a test that cannot fail, which is common in real suites.

questions.q: A test that uses randomly generated data fails about once a week and never on re-run. What makes it debuggable?
choices: Replace the random data with one fixed value, and delete the test if it still fails
Retry the test up to three times in CI, so a weekly failure no longer blocks merges
Generate data from a seeded generator and log the seed, so a failure can be replayed
Increase the amount of random data per run, so the failure shows up every time
questions.why: With the seed in the failure output you can rerun exactly the input that broke it, then turn it into a fixed regression case. Retrying hides a real bug, and fixing the data throws away the coverage randomness was giving you.
questions.asked: Tests whether you treat flaky tests as bugs to reproduce, not noise to retry.

questions.q: What is a consumer-driven contract test?
choices: An end-to-end test that deploys the consumer and provider together in one shared environment
A legal agreement on uptime between teams, checked by a monitor in production
A load test in which the consumer team sets the traffic the provider must handle
The consumer records the requests and responses it relies on; the provider's CI verifies them
questions.why: Each side tests alone against a shared contract (Pact is a well-known tool), so a provider change that breaks a consumer fails in the provider's pipeline before deploy. No shared end-to-end environment is needed, which is what makes it cheaper and faster than deploying both together.
questions.asked: Comes up once services are split between teams; the strong answer says which pipeline fails.

questions.q: What does mutation testing measure that line coverage does not?
choices: Whether tests fail when the code is deliberately altered, such as `>` turned into `>=`
How much memory the code allocates when the tests mutate shared objects between runs, in bytes
Whether the code still compiles after dependencies are upgraded to new versions
How often the test suite itself changes, as a signal of brittle tests
questions.why: A tool makes small changes (mutants) and reruns the suite; a mutant that survives shows code that runs under test but is not really checked. It is slow, so teams run it on critical modules rather than on every commit.
questions.asked: A depth question that follows "is 90% coverage good?"; it shows you know how to test the tests.

questions.q: The second test fails when the file runs, but passes when run on its own. Why?
choices: node:test runs tests in parallel, so both push to the array at the same moment
The tests share the module-level `cart`, so state from the first leaks into the second
`assert.equal` compares arrays by reference, so the length check reads a stale copy of it
The first test's assertion fails silently and leaves the runner in a broken state
questions.why: Tests in a file run in order by default and share module state, so 'starts empty' sees the apple. Create fresh state inside each test or in `beforeEach`. A test that passes only in a certain order is a flaky test waiting for a reordering.
questions.asked: Order dependence is the commonest cause of flaky suites; spotting it in five lines is the junior bar.
